stances.claim: The Mamasapano carnage is the most serious political crisis besetting PNoy since assumption -- but CJ agrees with the rage for truth and justice while believing there is no basis for resignation or ouster

For an Edsa-type rebellion to prosper, the military and the Church must combine -- neither is present for PNoy: private conversations with top CBCP officials show outright rejection of any ouster; Cardinal Tagle has openly discouraged any such move; CBCP has not been sounded out by any credible military commander

The FVR-Flor Contemplacion case (April 1994) is the most instructive precedent: when our people perceived palpable injustice against a Filipino OFW executed in Singapore, the fury welled up and threatened to unseat him -- only resolved when FVR proactively broke diplomatic ties with Singapore and 'forced' the resignations of two Cabinet members (Romulo and Confesor)

Gen. Almonte's 'Endless Journey' autobiography captures the scale of the Contemplacion outrage: 'the outpouring of grief was close to what we had felt and seen when Ninoy Aquino was assassinated' -- and only proactive resolution subdued the indignation

Other presidents have all faced serious crises -- Marcos's tarmac murder of Ninoy peacefully overwhelmed him; Cory subdued several coup attempts; Estrada's second-envelope-refusal triggered second Edsa and 'constructive resignation'; GMA's 'Hello Garci' nearly toppled her -- presidents invariably face serious political crises regardless of qualifications/intentions/accomplishments

How PNoy overcomes his crisis depends on how he satisfies the agonizing cries for truth and justice for the fallen SAF 44 -- publicly picking on subordinates will not alleviate the cries; public hand-washing and finger-pointing will just aggravate the agony

When our people perceive -- whether rightly or wrongly -- a palpable injustice, they rage until justice is done; Contemplacion was just one Filipino; in Mamasapano, 44 SAF officers perished -- the truth-and-justice imperative is proportionally greater

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes the Mamasapano carnage of January 25, 2015 -- in which 44 Special Action Force officers were killed -- as the most serious political crisis besetting President Aquino since he assumed office. Although PNP chief Alan Purisima has accepted full responsibility and resigned, many militants (including some bishops) and relatives of the deceased still press PNoy to own ultimate responsibility and resign. CJ agrees with the rage for truth and justice but believes there is no basis for the President's resignation, much less his ouster -- for an Edsa-type rebellion to prosper, the military and the Church must combine. Private conversations with top CBCP officials show an outright rejection of any kind of ouster; Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle, the highest-ranking Catholic prelate in the country, has openly discouraged any such move; none of the bishops, CJ understands, have been sounded out by any credible military commander to support a peaceful people-power revolt or an unconstitutional coup d'état. All that the CBCP officials ask for is transparency in arriving at the truth and in meting out justice to the culprits. The most instructive comparative crisis is the FVR-Flor Contemplacion case of April 1994. An overseas Filipino worker, Flor Contemplacion, was found guilty by a Singapore court of murdering Delia Maga, another OFW, and sentenced to death by hanging. Even after the verdict, friendly PH-Singapore relations continued; however, relations soured after Emilia Frenilla, another OFW, returned from the island-state and alleged that Contemplacion was innocent and that Maga's employer was the real killer. This late-breaking revelation sparked outrage among our people. FVR, under the theory of command responsibility, was blamed for the alleged injustice and for not doing enough to save Contemplacion. In his recent autobiography 'Endless Journey,' Gen. Jose T. Almonte, FVR's national security adviser, rued that 'the outpouring of grief was close to what we had felt and seen when Ninoy Aquino was assassinated.' To assuage the outrage, FVR asked the Singapore government to reopen the case so Frenilla could testify, but the request was turned down -- it was noted that a year before Contemplacion was executed, the Singaporean authorities had ignored a plea for compassion by the US government and penalized an American teenager by lashing him with a cane in addition to imprisoning him for four years for merely vandalizing cars. Because of this refusal, many Filipinos felt Contemplacion was denied a fair trial and that FVR did not do enough; after the OFW's execution, rallies and demonstrations became unstoppable and the 'fury welled-up, forming a tidal wave' that threatened to unseat FVR. Proactively, FVR broke diplomatic ties with Singapore and 'forced' the resignations of two Cabinet members: Foreign Affairs Secretary Roberto Romulo and Labor Secretary Nieves Confesor. Only then did the public indignation subside. Contemplacion was just one Filipino whom our people perceived to have been denied justice; in Mamasapano, 44 SAF officers perished. Truth and justice must be accorded them -- remembering that when our people perceive (rightly or wrongly) a palpable injustice, they rage until justice is done. Other chief executives have faced serious crises too. Marcos thought he fully controlled the country with an iron fist, but when our people perceived terrible injustice in the 'tarmac murder' of Ninoy Aquino, the masses rose peacefully and overwhelmed the dictator. Despite her herculean effort to restore democracy, the saintly Cory Aquino had to subdue several coup attempts. The perceived injustice at the Senate impeachment court's refusal to open the so-called 'second envelope' (supposed to contain damning evidence against President Estrada) triggered the second Edsa revolution that resulted in Estrada's 'constructive resignation' and his subsequent indictment, trial, and conviction for plunder. President GMA, who succeeded Estrada, initially did well -- until she mishandled the accusations of fraud during her 2004 electoral bid, especially when she perfunctorily confessed 'I am sorry' to the charge that she phoned an election commissioner to assure her victory. That notorious 'Hello Garci' incident, capped by the resignation of the 'Hyatt 10,' nearly toppled her; though she managed to finish her term, she is now detained -- despite her delicate medical condition -- while facing trial for plunder. The moral lesson from all these is that presidents, regardless of their qualifications, intentions, and accomplishments, invariably face serious political crises. How PNoy will overcome his own crisis depends on how he satisfies the agonizing cries for truth and justice for the fallen SAF 44. Publicly picking on subordinates will not alleviate the cries. Quite the contrary, such public hand-washing and finger-pointing will just aggravate the agony.
